In other news, as far as keywords on targets, it has very little to do with the game until it is brought up.  As much as I hate comparing this game to Magic:  The Gathering, it is like creature types versus creature cards.  Does it matter that your creature is a Lhurgoyf?  Not unless another card says "all Lhurgoyfs get +1/+1" or something to that effect.  Same goes with SotM targets.  Typically, it doesn't matter if your target is a Device, Appendage, The Law, or Cover.  It matters more that they are an Environment Target, Villain Target, Hero Target, or just a Target in general.  In Magic, it typically doesn't matter if your creature is an Elf/Frog/Ape/Dragon/etc. until another card brings it up, and classifying those creature types would fill a book the size of an alminac.  Typically, it just matters that it is a creature card.  Sure, sometimes "Citizen" or "Thoratian" cards are buffed, or "Gunmen" cards get DR equal to the number of "Cover" cards in play, but that's a deck-by-deck basis.  I think it would be very useful to include mention of specialized rules pertaining to individual decks (which, I believe, is already included in the rulebook, but I'm not sure), but including a glossary of every single type of target would only alienate and confuse new players rather than assist them in understanding the game.

It does not surprise me. MtG is a staple in the card game genre. The majority of people I know and have met through my time in this hobby have all played MtG extensivly at some point down the road (myself included). The comparison at some point is unavoidable. It is actually a GREAT jumping off point into the gameplay, as those who have played MtG will recognize the core mechanics of SotM immediatly and pick things up quickly.

The biggest difference, for me, is the fact that SotM is modular. 100%. It is this core difference that we should keep in mind when talking about these Keywords. What being a modular game allows is that special rules and mechanics can be isolated into these separate decks without them spilling out into the core game as a whole. This keeps the base games complexity fixed, eliminated the need for errata after every expansion release. And because new mechanics and rules are isolated within each deck, it is much less intimidating for new players as everything they need to know is on a deck-by-deck basis. Don't have The Block environment? Well thats ok because you wont see Agent cards anywhere else, so there is no need constantly refer to a big clunky list of terms.

The only confusion here is people wanting "keywords" as specifically defined within this game to mean the same thing as its defined within a completly separate game. It is an expectation that is rather unreasonable in my opinion.

posts.name: VicDiGital
posts.cooked:
(scratches head, mystified)

So... you don't see any benefit in having something clear and concise that shows up when someone does a search?  When it's as easy as just making a list?   Really?

Again, using my very first game as an example, randomly selecting heroes, villain and environment brought forth the Tumbleweed card as the very first environment card that we faced.  It had the word "Cover, Anomaly" on it, and an HP.  The Anomaly part made sense as that had to do with the time travel, but the Cover didn't.  There was no explanation of Cover in the main rules.  No explanation in the Shattered Timelines manual (that was the only expansion we had at the time).  We discussed it amongst ourselves:  "Was it a special sort of action that we had just missed in the rules, or was explained in a different expansion?"  Maybe we were all just stupid, and should have clearly figured out all the rules correctly from the first read-through before actually playing the game and experiencing all the cards as they were played.  I guess that's on us.  But all of us had come from various other card games such as Magic, Game of Thrones, Yu-Gi-Oh, Summoner Wars, where there ARE lots of different main keywords, and then sub-keywords and then faction keywords and special event keywords and on and on.  So it wasn't out of the realm of possibility that the the "cover' keyword triggered some other sort of ability that we were just too blind or stupid to see.  Wouldn't be the first time a rule was in plain sight and we kept reading it wrong or skimming over it.  

But even accounting for our stupidity, we did a search for ANY explanation or clarification of the "cover" keyword.  Nothing.  Nothing anywhere.  It's like the keyword didn't exist.  We went on without any sort of answer and I'm sure we played that wrong as well as all the other rules one plays wrong when learning a new game.  But afterwards, I made it a goal to find out what this keyword meant.  No matter where I looked or how deeply I delved into BGG or these forums, or the GTG website, there wasn't a single mention of what the cover keyword meant.  I searched for more than an hour.   Nothing.  

Maybe we're the only new players of this game who've ever wondered if there was more to a keyword than it seemed at first glance.  Or wondered if we were playing it right.  

The current list of non-essential keywords is only 75.  That's a tiny list.  One paragraph (like above) that brings all the similar non-essential keywords together.  Anyone who looks for one will find all the others, and will find instant clarification.   "This keyword is like these others."

And really, I love LOVE LOVE this game.  But when there's a 38 page errata/clarification document, CLEARLY the rules and card explanations aren't as straightforward and obvious as many people may want to believe, especially when you're learning the rules by yourself and not able to have someone who already knows the game there to explain it to you and answer questions.

posts.name: Reckless
posts.cooked:
VicDiGital:

(scratches head, mystified)So… you don't see any benefit in having something clear and concise that shows up when someone does a search?  When it's as easy as just making a list?   Really?

Keyword:  The words in the rectangular box at the top of any game text section.  Any keywords not defined in this glossary will make sense circumstantially.

 

Taken from the EE Rulebook PDF on the official SotM website.  Emphasis mine.

 

You had a rather unfortunate start to the keyword process (the Time Cataclysm is an environment deck from the third SotM expansion, Shattered Timelines, which is quite possibly the most storyline-intensive and reference-filled expansion in this whole game), and the circumstances of understanding the "Cover" keyword were in the "Silver Gulch" Promo Environment.  You didn't have the context for this keyword because you weren't familiar with another environment in the game that was released simultaneously with Shattered Timelines.  However, there are still cards in that deck with keywords that we cannot clearly identify from a certain deck (meaning they haven't been released yet).  It is very much meant to be a deck that combines elements from many Environment decks (past, present, and future) into one, fifteen card reference powerhouse.


Sentinels is a game that typically works best when you start with the Core and work your way up.  The characters are much easier to understand, for the most part (excluding Absolute Zero) and the villains help you understand turn order, card types, and cover many effects that are used throughout the game (damage, DR, buffing, types of damage, etc.).  For players who had started early on with the Core and worked toward Shattered Timelines, the references to "Dinosaur," Marsquake, Atlantean Throne Room, Surprise Shopping Spree, etc. in the Time Cataclysm would be understood as the four environments from the Core (Insula Primalis, Wagner Mars Base, Ruins of Atlantis, and Megalopolis, respectively).  The same goes for Rook City, Pike Industrial Complex, Realm of Discord, Tomb of Anubis, The Block, and (as mentioned) Silver Gulch (not sure if The Final Wasteland has one, now that I think of it).  Each deck has a card in TC.  The keywords Trial, Cover, etc. were cute little "winks" to the players who have played the previous expansions.

Just having the Core under your belt would've given a lot of context for what the Time Cataclysm deck's "deal" is.  It's a bunch of environments from Sentinels wrapped up into one, and sometimes the references stem from keywords previously used in them.  Dinosaur, for instance, is in there for fun.  Trials allow you to obtain Treasure cards in the Tomb of Anubis.  But there are no Treasure cards in Time Cataclysm.  It's just a reference.  If there was a keyword that wasn't recognized, a player with the Core set under their belt would assume that it was from a deck that they either hadn't played yet, or a deck that hasn't been released yet.  This deck isn't terribly helpful for new players, and I highly recommend you play as many of the other environments as you possibly can before you try to play in the Time Cataclysm again.  Precedent will help you greatly when playing many of the decks from Shattered Timelines because, as mentioned earlier, it is the third expansion in Sentinels of the Multiverse, and filled with references to previous sets.

That being said, there isn't anything wrong with an expanded Target Keyword glossary.  But the >G team is hard at work playtesting a brand-new game and a mega-expansion for Sentinels, so I think you're hope for a glossary will have to be granted by a kindly forum member with some extra time to spare for SotM.

I will disagree with you about magic. Using key words and understanding how those words interact with each other is meant to reward the devoted player. It takes a long time to fully understand how the cards interact and for players that have seen a certain keyword power before and know all the rulings about it there is a significant advantage. You see it is not just about the definition of the keyword, but about all the rulings about the keyword and how it interacts. There is nothing wrong with this in a competitive game. It is a company rewarding its base.
